hook: One war ended in under an hour.
facts: Britain and Zanzibar went to war on a morning in eighteen ninety-six.
The palace guns were old, and British ships opened fire from the harbour.
The whole war was over in about thirty-eight minutes, and it still counts.

hook: Napoleon once lost a fight to rabbits.
facts: His men set up a rabbit hunt to celebrate a peace treaty.
The rabbits were tame ones, so they ran towards people instead of away.
Hundreds of them swarmed the emperor, and he had to escape to his coach.

hook: One king ruled France for twenty minutes.
facts: His father gave up the throne during a revolution and handed it to him.
He spent the whole reign being pushed to sign his own papers of leaving.
He signed, and his rule ended before the ink on the first page was dry.

hook: Australia lost a war against birds.
facts: Farmers asked the army for help against huge flocks of emus eating crops.
Soldiers came with machine guns, but the birds split up and simply ran.
The army gave up twice, and the emus kept the farmland they had taken.

hook: Vikings never wore helmets with horns.
facts: Not one horned helmet has ever been dug up from a real Viking grave.
A costume designer put horns on stage singers in an opera long after.
The picture stuck so hard that the fake helmet is now the famous one.

hook: A dead pope once stood trial.
facts: A new pope had the body of an old one dug up and brought to court.
They dressed the corpse in robes and sat it on a chair to answer charges.
The dead man was found guilty, and a young helper spoke for him.

hook: Tug of war was an Olympic sport.
facts: Teams pulled a rope for medals at the Games for about twenty years.
Police officers from London won it twice while wearing their heavy boots.
It was dropped, so somewhere there are Olympic champions at pulling rope.

hook: The Olympics once gave medals for art.
facts: Painters, writers and musicians competed for gold beside the runners.
The rule was simple, in that every entry had to be about sport itself.
The man who restarted the Games even won a medal under a false name.

hook: People used to rent a pineapple.
facts: The fruit was so rare in Europe that only the very rich could buy one.
So shops let you hire one for an evening to carry to a grand party.
The same pineapple went from party to party until it began to rot.

hook: Ketchup was once sold as medicine.
facts: A doctor decided that tomatoes could cure stomach trouble and worse.
He sold his tomato mix as pills and claimed it fixed all kinds of pain.
The pills failed, but the sauce he made from them is in your fridge.

hook: Bubble wrap was invented as wallpaper.
facts: Two men sealed two shower curtains together and hoped for a new wall look.
Nobody wanted bumpy walls, so they tried selling it to keep plants warm.
Only later did someone wrap a computer in it, and the popping never stopped.

hook: Play-Doh started as a wallpaper cleaner.
facts: Coal heating left soot on walls, and this soft dough rubbed it off.
Then homes switched to cleaner heating and nobody needed the stuff.
A teacher used it for craft class, so the cleaner became a toy instead.

hook: The first computer programmer was a woman.
facts: She wrote steps for a machine that was never actually finished and built.
Her notes show a way to make it work through a whole list of numbers.
She saw that such a machine could handle music, not only sums.

hook: Quarantine comes from the word for forty.
facts: Ships arriving at Venice had to wait offshore before anyone could land.
The wait was forty days, and the local word for forty gave it its name.
So every time you say the word, you are counting days in old Italian.

hook: The word salary comes from salt.
facts: Salt was hard to get and was needed to keep meat from going bad.
Roman soldiers were given money that was tied to buying their salt.
The old word for salt money grew into the word on your pay slip.

hook: A jiffy is a real unit of time.
facts: People say it to mean soon, but scientists gave the word a real length.
In one field it means the time light takes to cross a tiny distance.
So a jiffy is far shorter than a blink, and you cannot wait just one.

hook: A nightmare was once a kind of demon.
facts: The second half of the word has nothing at all to do with horses.
It came from an old name for a spirit that sat on a sleeper's chest.
People felt the weight, could not move, and blamed the creature above them.

hook: English lost its word for two days ahead.
facts: There used to be a single word meaning the day after tomorrow.
It was overmorrow, and it sat neatly beside the word for two days back.
Both words faded, so now English needs three words where one would do.

hook: Typewriter is typed on one keyboard row.
facts: Every letter in the word sits on the top line of an ordinary keyboard.
Salesmen liked this, because they could type it fast without hunting.
It is the longest common word you can write without leaving that row.

hook: One country has no mosquitoes at all.
facts: Iceland has ponds and mild summers, so the insects should do well there.
But the ground freezes and thaws at odd times, breaking their life cycle.
Neighbouring lands are full of them, and nobody is sure why this one is not.

hook: One border runs through people's living rooms.
facts: Two towns on the Dutch and Belgian line are tangled inside each other.
Little pieces of one country sit inside the other, and some sit inside those.
White crosses mark the line on the pavement, and some cut houses in half.

hook: One country's flag is not a rectangle.
facts: Nepal flies two red triangles stacked on top of one another.
The shapes come from old banners carried by two different royal houses.
It is the only national flag on Earth with more than four sides.

hook: In Switzerland one guinea pig is illegal.
facts: The law treats these animals as social, so loneliness counts as harm.
You must keep at least two together, and a single one is not allowed.
When one dies, people rent a companion so the other is never alone.

hook: Russia and America are nearly touching.
facts: Two small islands sit in the sea between the two huge countries.
One belongs to each side, and only a narrow strip of water divides them.
The gap is small enough to see across, and in hard winters it can freeze.

hook: Africa sits in all four hemispheres.
facts: The line around the middle of the world cuts straight through it.
So does the line that splits east from west, and few places manage both.
That makes it the only continent to stand in every quarter at once.

hook: Ten days once vanished from the calendar.
facts: The old calendar had drifted, so the seasons no longer matched the dates.
To fix it, several countries simply deleted a run of days from October.
People went to sleep on the fourth and woke up on the fifteenth.

hook: September once really was the seventh month.
facts: Its name comes from the old word for seven, and October means eight.
The Roman year used to start in March, so the counting lined up then.
Two months were added near the start, and the names never caught up.

hook: Some minutes have sixty-one seconds.
facts: The Earth does not spin at a perfectly steady speed as it turns.
So timekeepers sometimes add one extra second to keep clocks honest.
It gets slipped in at the end of a day, and almost nobody notices.

hook: Most wasabi is not wasabi at all.
facts: The real plant grows slowly in cold running water and costs a fortune.
So most green paste is horseradish and mustard with colouring added.
Even in Japan, many restaurants serve the copy without saying so.

hook: Nutmeg was once worth more than gold.
facts: It grew on a tiny group of islands and nowhere else in the world.
Traders killed for control of them, and one was swapped for Manhattan.
Today the same spice sits in a cheap jar on a supermarket shelf.

hook: Vanilla comes from an orchid flower.
facts: The pod grows on a climbing orchid that opens for only one morning.
Outside its home, no insect knows how to pollinate it, so people do it.
Every bean is touched by hand, which is why real vanilla costs so much.

hook: Apples float because they are mostly air.
facts: About a quarter of the inside of an apple is empty space between cells.
That trapped air makes the fruit lighter than the water around it.
It is the reason a party game has you catching them with your teeth.

hook: People once paid taxes with chocolate beans.
facts: Cacao beans were used as money across much of ancient Central America.
A few beans bought food, and a larger pile could buy a whole animal.
People even faked them with clay, which makes chocolate an early forgery.

hook: The fortune cookie is not Chinese.
facts: It first appeared in America, most likely from Japanese bakers there.
Chinese restaurants took it up, and diners assumed it came from China.
When the cookies were later sold in China, they were called American.

hook: Pistachios can set themselves on fire.
facts: The nuts are oily, and when stored in bulk they slowly give off heat.
If the pile is too tight, that heat has nowhere at all to escape.
It builds until the load starts burning, so ships carry rules for them.

hook: Europeans once thought tomatoes were poison.
facts: Rich diners ate from plates made with lead, which the juice pulled out.
People fell ill after meals, and the bright red fruit took the blame.
It sat in gardens as decoration for years before anyone dared cook it.

hook: Carrots and night vision started as a lie.
facts: Wartime pilots were finding enemy planes at night with new secret radar.
To hide it, officials said the pilots simply ate a lot of carrots.
The story outlived the war, and parents still repeat it at dinner.

hook: One concert will last over six centuries.
facts: A church in Germany is playing one organ piece as slowly as possible.
It began at the turn of this century and is set to run for ages.
Chord changes are years apart, and crowds come just to hear one note shift.

hook: One famous piece of music is silence.
facts: The player walks on, sits down, and does not touch the keys at all.
It lasts a set time in three parts, and then the player simply stands.
The point is the room itself, so coughs and chairs become the music.

hook: One instrument is played without touching it.
facts: The theremin has two aerials and the player waves hands in the air.
One hand sets how high the note is, and the other sets how loud.
It made the wobbling sound in old films about space and monsters.

hook: A highway runs through an office building.
facts: A road in Osaka had to pass exactly where a tower was already planned.
Neither side would move, so they agreed the road would go straight through.
It crosses several floors, and the building is not connected to it at all.

hook: Venice stands on ancient wooden poles.
facts: Builders drove millions of tree trunks down into the soft mud below.
Under water with no air, the wood cannot rot in the usual way.
Minerals soaked in over centuries, so the poles slowly turned to stone.

hook: Roman concrete grows stronger in sea water.
facts: Modern concrete crumbles when salt water works its way into the cracks.
The Roman mix used volcanic ash, and sea water feeds a slow reaction.
New crystals grow inside the cracks, so the harbours healed themselves.

hook: Basketball was first played with fruit baskets.
facts: A teacher nailed two peach baskets to a railing to calm a rowdy class.
The bottoms were still in, so someone fetched the ball after every score.
It took years before anyone thought to simply cut the bottom out.

hook: Some old books are bound in human skin.
facts: Doctors and collectors did it, sometimes using the skin of the dead patient.
The practice even had a name, and a few such books survive in libraries.
Tests can now tell human skin from calf, and some famous ones were fakes.

hook: Paper money is not made of paper.
facts: Most banknotes are woven from cotton and linen, closer to cloth than paper.
That is why a note survives a wash and normal paper falls apart wet.
Some countries went further and now print money on thin sheets of plastic.

hook: One bank stores cheese as loan security.
facts: An Italian bank lends money to cheese makers who have no spare cash.
Instead of property, the farmer hands over wheels of hard cheese.
The bank keeps them in a guarded vault, turning them while they age.

hook: One country printed a hundred trillion note.
facts: Prices in Zimbabwe rose so fast that money lost value within hours.
The bank kept adding noughts until a single note reached that figure.
It could barely buy a bus ticket, and now collectors pay more for it.

hook: One island used giant stone discs as money.
facts: On Yap, wealth came as carved stone wheels taller than a grown person.
They were far too heavy to move, so nobody carried their money around.
Ownership just changed by agreement, and one sank at sea but still counted.

hook: Coins have ridges because of thieves.
facts: When coins were real silver, people shaved slivers off the smooth edges.
The coin still passed as whole, and the thief kept a pile of metal.
Ridges made shaving obvious, and we kept them long after the silver left.

hook: The largest living thing is a fungus.
facts: Under a forest in Oregon, one honey fungus spreads through the soil.
Most of it is hidden thread, and only the mushrooms show above ground.
It covers several square miles and has been growing for thousands of years.

hook: One forest is really a single tree.
facts: Thousands of aspen trunks in Utah look like an ordinary patch of woodland.
Underground they all share one root system, so they are one organism.
Every trunk turns the same colour on the same day, which gives it away.

hook: A seed sprouted after two thousand years.
facts: Diggers found old date palm seeds in a desert fortress and stored them.
Decades later someone planted one, mostly as a test, expecting nothing.
It grew, and a tree from a lost kind of palm is now alive again.

hook: One flower smells like rotting meat.
facts: The corpse flower can grow taller than a person before it opens.
It heats itself up to push the stink further across the forest floor.
The smell pulls in flies, which is the only way it gets pollinated.

hook: One plant counts before it snaps shut.
facts: A Venus flytrap has tiny hairs inside each half of its trap.
One touch does nothing, because rain and dust would waste the effort.
Two touches close it, and more touches tell it to start digesting.

hook: Grass grows from the bottom up.
facts: Most plants push out new growth from the very tip of each stem.
Grass grows from a point near the soil, so cutting the top does no harm.
That is why lawns survive mowing and why grazing animals never kill them.

hook: Pineapples do not grow on trees.
facts: The plant is low and spiky, closer to the ground than to your head.
One fruit sits in the middle of the leaves, like a candle on a holder.
It takes about two years, and the plant gives you only that one fruit.

hook: Some mushrooms glow in the dark.
facts: Dozens of kinds give off a soft green light after the sun goes down.
The glow comes from a slow chemical reaction inside the living tissue.
Sailors once called rotting glowing wood by the name of fox fire.

hook: Doctors still cannot fully explain anesthesia.
facts: We use it millions of times a year and it works almost every time.
But nobody can say exactly how the drugs switch awareness off and on.
We know which parts of the brain go quiet, not why that removes the self.

hook: Heroin was once sold as cough medicine.
facts: A large drug company put it on shelves as a safe syrup for children.
It was sold as the gentler choice, less habit forming than what came before.
That turned out to be badly wrong, and it took years to pull it back.

hook: The stethoscope was invented out of shyness.
facts: A doctor had to press his ear to a young woman's chest to hear the beat.
He felt awkward, so he rolled paper into a tube and listened through it.
The sound came through louder, and the rolled paper became a wooden tube.

hook: Doctors once refused to wash their hands.
facts: A young doctor noticed that mothers died far less when hands were cleaned.
He had no germ theory to explain it, so older doctors felt insulted.
They pushed him out, and he died before anyone accepted he was right.

hook: People once mailed their children by post.
facts: When parcel post began in America, the rules said nothing about people.
Parents stuck stamps on a child's coat and sent them to visit family.
A postal worker they knew walked them there, until new rules stopped it.

hook: A man with a flag once walked before cars.
facts: Early British law treated a car as a danger to horses and to people.
Someone had to walk ahead of it carrying a red flag as a warning.
The car had to crawl behind him, slower than an ordinary walking pace.

hook: Escalator used to be a brand name.
facts: One company owned the word and sold moving stairs under that label.
The name spread so widely that people used it for every make of stairs.
A court ruled it had become an ordinary word, and the company lost it.

hook: High heels were invented for men.
facts: Persian riders wore them so their boots gripped the stirrups better.
European noblemen copied the look to seem taller and more warlike.
Women took the style up later, and then men dropped it completely.

hook: The rivets on jeans came from miners.
facts: Working men kept tearing the pockets of their trousers under load.
A tailor added little metal studs at the corners where the cloth ripped.
The trousers stopped failing, and those studs are still on your jeans.

hook: Monopoly was made to warn about landlords.
facts: The first version was designed to show how rent drains everyone else.
Players were meant to feel how one owner slowly takes the whole board.
The lesson got lost, and the game became a way to enjoy being that owner.

hook: The teddy bear is named after a president.
facts: On a hunt, he refused to shoot a bear that others had tied to a tree.
A cartoon of the moment ran in the papers and people loved the story.
A shop owner made a toy bear, asked to use his name, and it stuck.

hook: The cube's inventor needed a month to solve it.
facts: He built it as a teaching model, not as a puzzle for people to beat.
Once he twisted it, he had no idea how to bring the colours back.
It took him weeks of work, and children now do it in under a minute.

hook: Lego bricks from long ago still fit.
facts: The shape of the brick was locked down more than sixty years ago.
Every piece since is cut to the same tiny margin, finer than a hair.
So a brick from your grandparents clicks onto one bought this morning.

hook: One scream appears in hundreds of films.
facts: A short recorded yell from an old western was kept in a sound library.
Editors kept reaching for the same clip whenever someone had to fall.
It is now in hundreds of films, and fans listen out for it as a joke.

hook: Old film snow was made of asbestos.
facts: Studios needed something white that drifted down slowly on camera.
Painted flakes of asbestos looked perfect and did not melt under lights.
Actors breathed it in for years before anyone understood the danger.

hook: Cinemas once banned popcorn.
facts: Early picture houses wanted to feel like grand theatres, not fairgrounds.
Popcorn was cheap street food, and the noise and mess were unwelcome.
Hard times changed their minds, because the snack made more money than tickets.

hook: In one town you cannot be buried.
facts: A settlement far north sits on ground that stays frozen all year round.
Bodies buried there never break down, and old ones stayed preserved.
So burials were stopped, and the seriously ill are flown south instead.

hook: One country banned chewing gum.
facts: Singapore grew tired of gum stuck on seats, floors and door sensors.
Selling it was made illegal, and bringing in a supply became an offence.
Gum for medical use is now allowed, but only from a pharmacy counter.

hook: One country's clock is forty-five minutes off.
facts: Most places set their time in whole hours away from the world standard.
Nepal chose a line running through its own land instead of a neighbour's.
That leaves it at an odd quarter-hour gap from everybody around it.

hook: One ocean is larger than all the land.
facts: The Pacific stretches so far that it covers about a third of the planet.
You could drop every continent and island into it and still have room.
From some points at sea, the nearest people are on a passing spacecraft.

hook: A tree in one desert bleeds red.
facts: The dragon tree grows like an umbrella turned inside out on dry rock.
Cut the bark and a dark red sap runs out and dries hard on the trunk.
It was traded for centuries as a dye and sold as the blood of dragons.

hook: Young sunflowers turn to follow the sun.
facts: The stem grows faster on one side during the day and swings the head east.
At night the other side catches up, so it faces sunrise by morning.
Once the flower opens fully it stops moving and holds one direction.

hook: One lake turns dead animals to stone.
facts: A lake in Tanzania is so salty and alkaline that few creatures survive.
Animals that die in it are coated in minerals rather than rotting away.
They dry into stiff stone-like shapes, and photographers pose them upright.

hook: One country gives books every Christmas Eve.
facts: In Iceland almost everyone hands over a book on that one evening.
Publishers save their best titles for a catalogue sent to every home.
The night is spent reading in bed, and it has a name of its own.

hook: The shortest English sentence is two letters.
facts: A sentence needs someone doing something, and usually that is two words.
But an order hides the person, so the doer does not have to be said.
That leaves the single word go, which is a whole grammatical sentence.

hook: One bird can copy a chainsaw.
facts: The lyrebird of Australia builds its song out of whatever it hears.
Males copy other birds, and near towns they add saws and car alarms.
One raised by people learned a flute tune and passed it to wild birds.

hook: A postal service once used rockets.
facts: Several countries tried firing mail across valleys and stretches of water.
One test in America launched a rocket full of letters at a warship.
It worked, but it cost far too much, so the idea was quietly dropped.

hook: One clock has no hands at all.
facts: A water clock in ancient times measured hours by a steady drip.
A bowl with a small hole sank at a known rate and marked the time.
Courts used them to limit speeches, which is where a time limit began.

hook: Wedding cake was once thrown at the bride.
facts: Roman guests broke a loaf of bread over the head of the new wife.
The crumbs were meant to bring luck and plenty to the new household.
Guests then grabbed the pieces, which slowly turned into serving slices.

hook: One prison escape used a rubber raft.
facts: Three men left Alcatraz through vents they had widened with spoons.
They left paper heads in their beds so the guards saw sleeping shapes.
Their raft was made of raincoats, and they were never found again.

hook: A city once banned pointed shoes.
facts: Fashion in the late Middle Ages pushed shoe tips to silly lengths.
Some were so long that walking upstairs became genuinely difficult.
Rulers set legal limits, with longer tips allowed only to the rich.

hook: One language has no words for left.
facts: Some Aboriginal Australian speakers use compass directions for everything.
They will say there is an ant on your south leg, not on your left leg.
Speakers keep a sense of direction from childhood, even indoors.

hook: The first computer bug was a real moth.
facts: A huge early machine started giving wrong answers for no clear reason.
Engineers opened it up and found a moth stuck between two contacts.
They taped the insect into the logbook and wrote that they had debugged it.

hook: The at sign is far older than email.
facts: Traders used it for centuries to mean each, as in six barrels at one price.
It sat unloved on typewriters for decades with almost nothing to do.
An engineer picked it because no name could ever contain it by accident.

hook: The first webcam watched a coffee pot.
facts: Researchers were tired of walking to the kitchen to find an empty jug.
They pointed a camera at the pot and piped the picture to their screens.
Once it went online, people all over the world watched that coffee brew.

hook: Wi-Fi came from looking for black holes.
facts: Astronomers in Australia were trying to pick out faint signals from space.
They built maths to clean up echoes that smeared the signal in a room.
That same trick is what lets your router work through walls today.

hook: The letters S O S stand for nothing.
facts: People say it means save our ship, but that was invented afterwards.
It was chosen because in Morse code it is three dots, three dashes, three dots.
That pattern is easy to send in a panic and hard to mistake for anything.

hook: The first text message said Merry Christmas.
facts: An engineer sent it from a computer, because phones could not yet type.
It went to a colleague at a party who had no way at all to reply.
Short messages were meant as a minor extra, not as the main use.

hook: One phone giant started as a paper mill.
facts: Nokia began beside a river in Finland, grinding wood into pulp.
It later made rubber boots, car tyres and cables for many years.
Only near the end of the last century did it turn fully to phones.

hook: Bluetooth is named after a Viking king.
facts: A Danish king united warring tribes, and he had a famously dark tooth.
Engineers wanted a name for a standard that would unite rival devices.
Even the symbol is his two initials in old runes, laid on top of each other.

hook: Old window glass is not slowly flowing.
facts: People say old panes are thicker at the bottom because glass creeps down.
In truth the old method made uneven sheets, and fitters put the thick edge low.
Glass at room temperature would need longer than the universe to sag.

hook: Helium was found on the sun before Earth.
facts: During an eclipse, astronomers saw a colour that matched no known element.
They named it after the Greek word for sun and waited to find it here.
Nearly thirty years passed before anyone dug any of it out of the ground.

hook: One metal melts in your hand.
facts: Gallium is a solid on the shelf and looks a lot like polished silver.
Hold a lump in your palm and body heat alone turns it into a puddle.
Pranksters cast it into spoons that vanish when stirred into hot tea.

hook: Aluminium was once worth more than gold.
facts: The metal is common in rock but was extremely hard to pull out of it.
An emperor served his best guests on aluminium while others got gold.
A new method made it cheap, and now it is thrown away as foil.

hook: Rubber was useless until someone burned it.
facts: Natural rubber turned sticky in summer and cracked hard in winter.
An inventor spent years failing, then dropped a mix onto a hot stove.
The heat locked it into something springy that held its shape in any weather.

hook: Purple dye once came from sea snails.
facts: It took many thousands of shellfish to colour a single royal robe.
The workshops stank so badly that they were pushed outside the city walls.
That is why purple meant power, since almost nobody could afford it.

hook: The first bright purple dye was an accident.
facts: A teenage chemist was trying to make a malaria treatment in his holidays.
He got a black sludge, and rinsing it left a brilliant purple stain.
He dropped medicine, sold the colour, and made himself very rich.

hook: Some places have not seen rain for centuries.
facts: Parts of the Atacama in Chile are the driest ground outside the poles.
Mountains on both sides block wet air before it can ever arrive.
The soil is so dry and dead that spacecraft are tested there for Mars.

hook: One volcano burns with blue flames.
facts: A crater in Indonesia glows an electric blue all through the night.
The lava is normal, but sulphur gas catches fire as it escapes cracks.
Miners walk in with baskets and carry the cooled yellow lumps out.

hook: One fire has burned for thousands of years.
facts: On a hillside in Turkey, flames come straight out of the bare rock.
Gas seeps up from below and lights the moment it meets the air.
Ancient sailors used the glow to steer, and it has never gone out.

hook: Everest gets taller every single year.
facts: India is still pushing north into Asia and crumpling the ground upward.
The whole range rises by a few millimetres over the course of a year.
Earthquakes can undo some of it, so the official height keeps changing.

hook: Desert dust feeds a rainforest across an ocean.
facts: Wind lifts fine dust off the Sahara and carries it over the Atlantic.
The dust is rich in the exact mineral the Amazon soil keeps losing to rain.
Millions of tonnes fall every year, so one desert fertilises one jungle.

hook: A lake sits under the Antarctic ice.
facts: Far below the surface, liquid water is trapped against the bedrock.
The weight of the ice above and heat from below stop it freezing solid.
It has been sealed off for millions of years, and life may still be in it.

hook: Iceland is being pulled apart every year.
facts: The island sits right on the seam where two great plates move away.
One half drifts towards America and the other towards Europe.
You can walk down into the gap and touch both sides at the same time.

hook: Ancient Olympic athletes wore no clothes.
facts: Competitors oiled their skin and took part completely bare.
One story says a runner lost his shorts, won, and started the habit.
The word gymnasium comes straight from their word for naked.

hook: A royal family chose the marathon distance.
facts: The old race had no fixed length, and the number kept changing.
For the London games the start was moved so the royals could watch it.
That odd distance was later frozen as the rule, and we still run it.

hook: Golf balls fly farther because they are dented.
facts: Players noticed that old scuffed balls travelled better than new smooth ones.
The dents hold a thin layer of turning air close against the surface.
That cuts the drag behind the ball, so makers began cutting them on purpose.

hook: A football match helped start a real war.
facts: Two neighbours in Central America met in a bad tempered qualifying tie.
Anger over land and migration had been building for years before it.
Fighting broke out days after the last match, and the name stuck.

hook: One cricket match lasted twelve days unfinished.
facts: The two teams agreed to play on with no time limit until someone won.
Rain kept washing out play, and the scores crept along for nearly two weeks.
In the end the visitors had to leave to catch their ship home.

hook: Van Gogh sold almost nothing while alive.
facts: He painted hundreds of works in about ten years of very hard effort.
His brother sent him money and tried to interest dealers, with little luck.
Today a single one of those canvases can change hands for a fortune.

hook: The Mona Lisa got famous after being stolen.
facts: It was a respected painting, but far from the best known in the world.
A workman walked out of the Louvre with it hidden under his coat.
The empty wall drew crowds for two years, and the fame never faded.

hook: One painting shredded itself after being sold.
facts: The artist had built a cutter into the frame years before the sale.
The moment the hammer fell, the canvas slid down through the blades.
It stopped halfway, and the half shredded work became worth even more.

hook: Michelangelo hated painting that famous ceiling.
facts: He thought of himself as a sculptor and said painting was not his trade.
He worked standing, bent backwards, with plaster dripping onto his face.
He wrote a bitter poem about it while he was still up on the boards.

hook: Ancient writers almost never mention blue.
facts: Old Greek texts call the sea wine dark and describe sheep as violet.
Cultures name colours in a rough order, and blue tends to arrive last.
There was almost nothing naturally blue to point at and give a name.

hook: The Statue of Liberty used to be brown.
facts: It is built from thin copper sheets, the colour of a shiny new coin.
Sea air slowly ate at the surface and grew a thin crust over it.
That crust is green, and it now protects the metal underneath.

hook: One country drives on both sides.
facts: Most nations pick a side of the road and keep to it everywhere.
A short bridge on the Chinese border must swap traffic over as it crosses.
Cars cross over on a looping ramp so both systems can meet safely.

hook: A river once caught fire.
facts: Factories along an American river poured oil and waste straight into it.
The slick on the surface was thick enough to light and it burned.
It happened more than once, and the shame pushed through clean water laws.

hook: One island has more sheep than people.
facts: The Falklands keep a flock many times the size of the human population.
The land is windy grass, which suits wool far better than crops.
New Zealand once had a similar gap, though it has narrowed a lot.

hook: The unluckiest man survived two atom bombs.
facts: He was in Hiroshima on business when the first bomb went off nearby.
Burned but alive, he took a train home to Nagasaki to recover.
He was back at work describing the blast when the second one landed.

hook: A tortoise outlived everyone who found it.
facts: One was taken from the wild during the age of sailing ships.
It passed through several owners and outlasted every one of them.
It was still eating grass in a zoo after well over a century.

hook: The word robot means forced labour.
facts: It was invented for a stage play in Czech, not by any engineer.
The root word means the hard work owed by a peasant to a lord.
In that play the machines revolt, so the warning came with the name.

hook: One machine ran on punched cards from weaving.
facts: A loom used stiff cards with holes to set the pattern in the cloth.
Early computers borrowed the very same idea to hold their instructions.
So the way a jumper was patterned became the way a machine was told what to do.

hook: Barcodes were first drawn in sand.
facts: An inventor sat on a beach thinking about how to label a tin of soup.
He pulled his fingers through the sand and left a set of lines.
That doodle became the striped code now scanned on almost everything.

hook: One car company began making looms.
facts: Toyota started life building automatic weaving machines for cloth.
The founder sold the rights to his best loom to fund something new.
That money paid for the first cars, and the family name stayed.

hook: Traffic lights existed before cars did.
facts: London put up a gas lit signal to control horses and carts by the bridge.
A policeman worked the arms by hand to hold one direction at a time.
It exploded after a few weeks, and the idea waited fifty years to return.

hook: Crows remember faces and hold grudges.
facts: Researchers wearing masks caught a few crows and then let them go.
Birds that had never been caught still scolded that mask years later.
The parents had taught the young ones which face to shout at.

hook: One animal makes cube shaped droppings.
facts: The wombat is the only creature known to produce square sided waste.
Its gut has stiff and stretchy patches that press the shape as it moves.
Cubes do not roll away, so they stay put as a scent marker on rocks.

hook: Pigeons can tell one painter from another.
facts: Birds were shown paintings and rewarded for pecking at one artist only.
They soon sorted new pictures they had never seen into the right pile.
So a pigeon can pass a test that many gallery visitors would fail.

hook: Goats have rectangular eyes.
facts: The dark part of a goat's eye is a wide horizontal slot, not a circle.
That shape gives a very broad view for spotting movement to the sides.
The eyes even rotate as the head lowers, so the slot stays level.

hook: Some snails sleep for three whole years.
facts: In hot dry spells a snail seals its shell with a plug of dried slime.
Inside it slows almost to a stop and simply waits for the weather.
If the rain takes years to come, the snail can wait that long.

hook: Cows have best friends.
facts: Farmers noticed that certain pairs graze and lie down together daily.
Split those two apart and the heart rate of both animals climbs.
Kept with a friend, a cow feeds better and gives more milk.

hook: A horse physically cannot be sick.
facts: The muscle where the gullet meets the stomach is unusually strong.
It works one way only, so food goes down but nothing comes back up.
This is why a bad stomach can turn deadly for a horse very fast.

hook: Owls cannot move their eyes at all.
facts: The eyes are long tubes, not balls, so they are locked into the skull.
To look sideways the whole head has to swing round instead.
Extra bones in the neck let an owl turn much further than we can.

hook: Reindeer eyes change colour in winter.
facts: A layer behind the eye is a rich gold through the bright summer months.
As the long dark arrives, that same layer shifts to a deep blue.
The blue scatters light inside the eye and helps them see in gloom.

hook: The narwhal horn is really a tooth.
facts: What looks like a spear is a single tooth pushed out through the lip.
It is packed with nerve endings, so the tusk can actually sense things.
Now and then a narwhal grows two, which means two front teeth outside.

hook: Squirrels plant forests by being forgetful.
facts: One animal buries thousands of nuts across a wide patch of ground.
It never finds them all again, and the forgotten ones are left alone.
Those buried seeds sprout, so much of a wood is planted by mistake.

hook: Male seahorses are the ones who give birth.
facts: The female places her eggs into a pouch on the front of the male.
He fertilises them inside, then carries and feeds them until they are ready.
When the time comes he pumps and tiny seahorses shoot out of the pouch.

hook: A crocodile cannot stick out its tongue.
facts: A band of skin holds the tongue flat against the floor of the mouth.
So the huge jaws open wide and the tongue never comes forward at all.
It also stops water pouring down the throat while the mouth is open.

hook: An ostrich eye is bigger than its brain.
facts: Each eye is about the size of a billiard ball, the largest of any land animal.
The brain behind it is smaller than that, which is unusual for a bird.
The trade seems worth it, since it can spot a lion very far off.

hook: Snakes hear through their jawbones.
facts: A snake has no outer ear opening at all on either side of the head.
Sound travels through the ground and into the bone of the lower jaw.
From there it reaches the inner ear, so the snake hears by feeling.

hook: People once slept in two separate shifts.
facts: Before cheap lighting, many went to bed early and woke near midnight.
They prayed, talked or visited neighbours for an hour in the dark.
Then they went back down for a second sleep until the sun came up.

hook: A dirty plate gave the world penicillin.
facts: A scientist left his samples out while he went away on holiday.
He came back to a mouldy dish and noticed a clear ring around the mould.
The bacteria had died there, and that ring became the first antibiotic.

hook: A famous sauce is made from rotted fish.
facts: Worcestershire sauce starts with salted anchovies left to break down.
The story goes that a failed first batch was abandoned in a cellar.
Tasted again much later, it had turned into something people loved.

hook: The croissant is not originally French.
facts: Its ancestor is an Austrian pastry baked in the shape of a crescent.
A Viennese baker opened a shop in Paris and brought the shape with him.
French bakers then rebuilt it with layered butter dough, and it took over.

hook: One spread is left over from making beer.
facts: Brewing leaves behind a thick sludge of spent yeast at the bottom.
A scientist worked out that this waste could be turned into food paste.
So a strong salty spread on toast is really a brewery by-product.

hook: Chilli does not actually burn you.
facts: The heat comes from a chemical that grips the nerve for real warmth.
The nerve fires, so the brain is told there is heat when there is none.
Birds lack that sensor entirely, which is how they spread the seeds.

hook: Onions attack you with a tiny gas.
facts: Cutting one breaks cells that keep two chemicals carefully apart.
They mix, and the reaction throws off a gas that drifts up to your eyes.
Tears are your eye rinsing away a mild acid it has just made.

hook: The sandwich is named after a gambler.
facts: An English earl did not want to leave the card table to eat a meal.
He asked for meat between two slices so he could hold it in one hand.
Others began ordering the same as him, and the name is his title.

hook: Boycott was the name of a real man.
facts: He managed land in Ireland and pushed hard on the tenant farmers.
The whole community agreed to stop dealing with him in any way.
Shops refused him, workers walked off, and his surname became the verb.

hook: Silhouette was a hated finance minister.
facts: He taxed the rich and pushed cheap living during a costly war.
People sneered that anything done on the cheap was done his way.
A shadow outline was the cheapest portrait, so it took his name.

hook: The word nice once meant stupid.
facts: It came from a root meaning not knowing, so it began as an insult.
Over centuries it drifted through fussy, then shy, then pleasant.
Almost no other English word has swung so far from where it started.

hook: In some countries a mouse takes the tooth.
facts: Children in Spain and much of Latin America do not wait for a fairy.
A small mouse is said to come for the tooth and leave a coin behind.
In France the same visitor is a mouse too, with its own old name.

hook: Europe resisted the number zero for centuries.
facts: Merchants using Roman numerals had no symbol for nothing at all.
When the idea arrived from India, some cities banned it outright.
They feared a digit that changed value could be used to fake ledgers.

hook: A child named one of the biggest numbers.
facts: A mathematician asked his young nephew what to call a huge figure.
The boy made up a nonsense word on the spot, and it was adopted.
A famous search company later built its own name from that word.

hook: The Eiffel Tower was meant to be temporary.
facts: It was put up as the entrance arch for a fair and given a short licence.
Artists signed a letter calling it a useless and monstrous chimney.
It was saved because the army found it perfect for radio aerials.

hook: Big Ben is a bell, not the tower.
facts: The name belongs to the great bell that hangs high inside the clock.
The tower itself was called the Clock Tower for most of its life.
It was renamed for a royal jubilee, but still not Big Ben.

hook: The Pompeii bodies are hollow plaster casts.
facts: Ash buried the town and hardened around people before they broke down.
That left empty spaces in the rock exactly the shape of each person.
Diggers poured plaster into the holes, so the figures are casts of air.

hook: One flower bulb once cost a whole house.
facts: Rare tulips became a craze in the Netherlands and prices went wild.
People traded contracts for bulbs still buried in the winter ground.
The market collapsed in weeks, and buyers were left holding onions.

hook: A woman went over Niagara in a barrel.
facts: She was a teacher with no money and no experience of stunts at all.
She padded a wooden barrel, climbed in, and had the lid screwed down.
She survived, made very little money, and warned others never to try.

hook: A stray dog became the first space traveller.
facts: She was picked up from the streets of Moscow and trained in weeks.
Engineers chose strays because they already coped with cold and hunger.
She reached orbit, and there was never any plan to bring her home.

hook: One airline flight lasts under two minutes.
facts: Two islands in Scotland are linked by a scheduled flight in a small plane.
The hop between them is shorter than the runway at many big airports.
With a good wind behind it, the whole journey can take under a minute.

hook: One hotel is built entirely out of salt.
facts: It stands on a vast dried salt flat high in the mountains of Bolivia.
Walls, floors, chairs and beds are all cut from blocks of salt.
Guests are asked not to lick the walls, which apparently needs saying.

hook: One library book came back after a century.
facts: A borrower took it out and it simply stayed on a family shelf.
A descendant found it while clearing a house and posted it back.
The library waived the fine, which would have been an absurd sum.

hook: One Swiss town has banned cars for ever.
facts: Zermatt sits under the Matterhorn and allows no petrol cars at all.
Visitors park in the next village down and finish the trip by train.
Inside the town everything moves by small electric cart or by horse.

hook: Saudi Arabia has no permanent rivers.
facts: The whole country contains not one river that flows all year round.
Rain runs down dry valleys for a few hours and then vanishes.
Most drinking water is pulled from the sea and the salt taken out.

hook: The oldest known complaint is on clay.
facts: A customer in ancient Mesopotamia was sent the wrong grade of copper.
He pressed his anger into a clay tablet and had it delivered.
It survives, so the earliest complaint we have is about bad metal.

hook: Shakespeare put hundreds of words into English.
facts: He needed words that did not exist, so he bent old ones into new shapes.
Many first appear in print in his plays and never left the language.
Some he only popularised, but the list of firsts is still enormous.

hook: Some baobabs died after standing a thousand years.
facts: The baobab stores water in a trunk wide enough to hollow into a room.
Some of the oldest ones have died suddenly in the last few decades.
Trees that stood for over a thousand years fell within a single year.

hook: A whole town lives inside one building.
facts: In an Alaskan town, nearly every resident sleeps in the same block.
The school, the shop and the offices are joined on to the same structure.
In deep winter you can live a full week without stepping outdoors.

hook: One bridge is grown, not built.
facts: In north east India, people guide the roots of fig trees across rivers.
The roots are trained along frames for years until they reach the far bank.
The bridge then keeps growing, so it gets stronger instead of rotting.

hook: A failed red paint created the first blue.
facts: A workshop was boiling bones and waste to make a red pigment.
Something in the pot was contaminated and the batch came out deep blue.
That accident gave painters the first strong blue they could afford.

hook: A tiny country was founded on a sea fort.
facts: An old wartime platform stands on stilts off the coast of England.
A family moved on, declared it a nation, and printed their own stamps.
No large country recognises it, but they have run it for decades.

hook: One plant can hear itself being eaten.
facts: Researchers played the recorded sound of a caterpillar chewing leaves.
The plant heard the vibration and pushed out more of its defence chemicals.
Wind and insect song caused no such reaction, so it knew the difference.

hook: An entire lake vanished down a hole.
facts: A lake in Louisiana sat above an old salt mine being dug underneath.
A drill punched through the roof and opened a drain into the tunnels.
The water spun down, swallowed barges, and briefly ran a river backwards.
